catalog_quote: Stress placement is predictable occurring on the last syllable. Disyllabic words have a short minor presyllable consisting of CV(N) or a syllabic nasal N̩. ... 2.2 Stress. Most So words are monosyllabic. On disyllabic words, however, the stress is usually on the second (or major) syllable. The preceding short minor syllable is unstressed. That is, the phonological word is composed of: Phonological Word (PW) (σ) 'σ. Thus an optional unstressed preceding syllable (σ) may occur before the main stressed syllable ('σ). The following So examples reflect this disyllabic pattern of stress placement. The period (σ.σ) marks the boundary between syllables. ku.'ci:t die; ʔa.'ci:t to kill; ʔa.'baŋ to hide something; ma.'na:ŋ sun; pa.'ni̤c bamboo shoots; ra.'bɑh beak; tʰa.'nṳ: a bow (weapon); ta.'bɯ: evening; ba.'daŋ wonder; ca.'ri̤ak buffalo; ha.'mɑ how much; ci.'wa:c pull back; pʰa.'ɲa: word; sa.'b…

new_statements.quote: Word forms are mostly monosyllabic and disyllabic. Disyllabic words have stress on the second syllable so that the phonological word consists of (σ) + 'σ, i.e., an optional first syllable followed by a stressed second syllable. [...] Stress. Most So words are monosyllabic. On disyllabic words, however, the stress is usually on the second (or major) syllable. The preceding short minor syllable is unstressed. Thus an optional unstressed preceding syllable (σ) may occur before the main stressed syllable ('σ). [...] So is predominantly sesquisyllabic with stress placement on the final syllable of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in a disyllable the final (major) syllable carries the stress and the preceding minor presyllable (CV(N) or syllabic nasal, vowel restricted to /a i u/, clear register only) is unstressed and reduced. Stress is thus word-final and non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (words are at most two syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'usually' on the second syllable; no counter-examples given. Minor-syllable vowel shows free variation short~long. Lerthirunwong 1980:20 adds that a ʔaʔ presyllable may be dropped altogether, leaving a monosyllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (citation forms); the language also has a two-way register (clear vs breathy phonation) contrast on the major syllable, not tone. Variety: So of Kusuman District, Sakon Nakhon (the prestige dialect on the Thai side). Same rule stated independently in Lerthirunwong 1980 sec. 0.8 (also Kusuman).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the So (/thrò:/, autonym lakuay thro:) of Kusuman District, Sakon Nakhon Province, NE Thailand = Glottolog sooo1254 [sss]. Caution on Glottolog's bibliography for this languoid: per Migliazza 2003:69-70, Kulachol 1986 and Jungprasert 1986 ('So' of Dong Luang, Mukdahan) actually describe a Bru variety (Eastern/Western Bru, not sooo1254), and Suwilai 1996 'So (Thavung)' is Thavung (Vietic, thav1234), a different language altogether.

B 'Overview of So phonology' (p.71) and subsection 'Stress' (p.72): words mostly mono- or disyllabic; disyllables have an unstressed short minor presyllable CV(N) or syllabic nasal plus a stressed major syllable, (σ)+'σ; 'stress is usually on the second (or major) syllable'; 'So is predominantly sesquisyllabic with stress placement on the final syllable of the word'. Examples ku.'ci:t 'die', ʔa.'ci:t 'to kill', ca.'riak 'buffalo'.

sources.note: Sec. 0.8 'Stress' (thesis p.20; scan has clipped left margin): 'The majority of the words of So are monosyllabic. On disyllabic [words] it is usually the second of the disyllabic forms which is stressed, [resulting] in the shortening of the unstressed first syllable. ku:ci:t -> kŭʔci:t "die". The disyllabic words having ʔaʔ as the first syllable may have to drop the first syllable, resulting in a monosyllabic form.' Also sec. 0.7 Register: two registers, clear (mid level pitch) vs breathy (low rising pitch).
